meta.title: Who really said "For the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — George Eliot wrote it. It is the closing sentence of the Finale of Middlemarch (1871–72), about Dorothea Brooke. The popular version quietly re-capitalizes a mid-sentence "for."

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely George Eliot: the last sentence of Middlemarch's Finale (1871–72), on Dorothea Brooke. The popular quote trims its opening clause and capitalizes "For."

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: Pen name of Mary Ann Evans, 1819–1880 · English novelist
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing words of the “Finale” of Middlemarch (published in eight parts, 1871–72), Eliot’s summation of the quietly consequential life of her heroine Dorothea Brooke. The wording is genuine and confirmed against the full text — though the popular version begins mid-sentence: the novel reads “…incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world…” with a lowercase “for.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life

source.excerpt: Her finely touched spirit had still its fine issues, though they were not widely visible. Her full nature, like that river of which Cyrus broke the strength, spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth. But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.
trail: Web sources uniformly place the line in the “Finale” of George Eliot’s Middlemarch, as Eliot’s parting reflection on Dorothea Brooke.
We confirmed the exact wording against the full text at Standard Ebooks, which shows the line closes the novel’s final sentence.
A second independent full text at The Literature Page matches word-for-word, including the lower-case “for” that the popular quote re-capitalizes.
source.excerptNote: The famous line is the final clause; “you and me” is the narrator addressing the reader directly about Dorothea’s hidden influence.

source.rightsNote: Middlemarch was first published in 1871–72 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so the text is in the public domain. George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) died in 1880, and the work is long out of copyright worldwide.

author.bio: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. Her masterpiece, Middlemarch (1871–72), is a panoramic study of provincial life whose closing meditation on quiet, unrecorded goodness is among the most quoted passages in English fiction. She wrote under a male name to be taken seriously and to distance her fiction from her unconventional private life.

misattribution.heading: A wording note
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely George Eliot — but the version that circulates has been quietly trimmed and re-punctuated from the original sentence.

items.why: The popular quote starts “For the growing good of the world…” with a capital F. In the novel it is a lower-case “for” continuing the sentence “But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world…” (Standard Ebooks).
Detached from the novel, the line reads as a general aphorism. In place it is Eliot’s narrator summing up the diffuse, unseen good done by Dorothea Brooke specifically.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is correct and the words are Eliot’s own — it is the last sentence of Middlemarch’s Finale; only the opening capital “For” and the missing lead-in clause are cosmetic changes.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The sentence closes Middlemarch by refusing its heroine a grand public destiny and insisting that her worth lies elsewhere. Dorothea Brooke never becomes a Saint Theresa or an Antigone; her nature, Eliot writes, “spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth.” The final clause reframes that apparent smallness as the very engine of human progress.

It has become a secular benediction — quoted at funerals, in sermons, and in tributes to ordinary lives — precisely because it dignifies the unrecorded and the forgotten. That resonance is why it now travels far from the page, usually shorn of Dorothea and beginning with a capitalized “For.”
context.pull: “…the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.”
